title: Middle Kingdom and the Hyksos
subtitle: 2100–1550 BC · Reunification, the Classic State, and the Foreign Kings of the Delta

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: From Mentuhotep II's reunification through the Twelfth Dynasty's classic state to its fracture and the Hyksos kingdom in the Delta

entries.label: Mentuhotep II — reunifier of Egypt
entries.hint: Nebhepetre Mentuhotep II ruled Thebes through the last phase of the civil war against Herakleopolis and, by about his 39th regnal year, held the whole Nile Valley again — the reunification that opens the Middle Kingdom. He marked the change by taking the Horus name Sematawy ('Uniter of the Two Lands') and built a terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, a new architectural form that Hatshepsut's architects would echo five centuries later.
entries.note: Deir el-Bahari temple excavated by Édouard Naville (Egypt Exploration Fund, 1903–07) and Herbert Winlock (Metropolitan Museum, 1920s). Regnal-year change of titulary: relief fragments from Gebelein and Deir el-Ballas. Synthesis: Grajetzki, The Middle Kingdom of Ancient Egypt (2006) pp.19–25; Shaw (ed.), Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000) pp.151–57.

entries.label: Mentuhotep III and IV — the end of the Eleventh Dynasty
entries.hint: Sankhkare Mentuhotep III sent his steward Henenu on a large expedition through the Wadi Hammamat to the Red Sea and on to Punt, and fortified the eastern approaches to Thebes. His successor Nebtawyre Mentuhotep IV is absent from the later king-lists — the Turin Canon marks 'seven kingless years' here — yet a Wadi Hammamat inscription of his Year 2 records a quarrying expedition of 10,000 men led by his vizier, one Amenemhat, widely thought to be the future Amenemhat I.
entries.note: Henenu's expedition: rock inscription in the Wadi Hammamat (Couyat & Montet, Les inscriptions hiéroglyphiques du Ouâdi Hammâmât, 1912, no.114). Mentuhotep IV's Year 2 inscription: Wadi Hammamat no.110 and the 'well' and 'gazelle' wonder-texts. Turin Canon column 5. Grajetzki (2006) pp.26–27.

entries.label: Amenemhat I — founder of the Twelfth Dynasty
entries.hint: Sehetepibre Amenemhat I, most likely the vizier of the same name, took the throne without royal descent and rebuilt the state around a new residence, Amenemhat-itj-tawy ('Amenemhat seizes the Two Lands'), near modern el-Lisht at the junction of Upper and Lower Egypt. He installed his son Senwosret I as co-regent — the first attested Egyptian co-regency — and was killed in a palace conspiracy while Senwosret was campaigning in Libya, an event refracted through the Story of Sinuhe and the Instruction of Amenemhat.
entries.note: Co-regency and assassination: Story of Sinuhe (Berlin 3022 and Ashmolean fragments) and the Instruction of Amenemhat I (P. Millingen and school copies), both in Parkinson, The Tale of Sinuhe and Other Ancient Egyptian Poems 1940–1640 BC (1997). Pyramid and residence: Dieter Arnold, The Pyramid of Senwosret I / The South Cemeteries of Lisht (MMA, 1988–92). Grajetzki (2006) pp.28–34.

entries.label: Senwosret I — the conquest of Lower Nubia
entries.hint: Kheperkare Senwosret I pushed the Egyptian frontier to the Second Cataract, garrisoning Buhen and building or enlarging a chain of forts along the Nubian Nile to control the gold roads and the river traffic. At home he ran one of the most ambitious building programmes of any Egyptian king — a rebuilt temple of Amun-Ra at Karnak, of which the finely carved 'White Chapel' survives — and left the Berlin Leather Roll, a dedication text arguing the theology of royal temple-building.
entries.note: Buhen and the fort chain: excavated by W.B. Emery (Egypt Exploration Society, 1957–64). Girgawi/Buhen stela of the general Mentuhotep (year 18). White Chapel: reconstructed at Karnak from talatat reused in the Third Pylon. Berlin Leather Roll (P. Berlin 3029). Grajetzki (2006) pp.35–41.

entries.label: Amenemhat II — the Mit Rahina annals
entries.hint: Nubkaure Amenemhat II is thinly attested in monuments but unusually well documented in one text: a fragmentary annal-stone reused at Memphis (Mit Rahina) that logs, year by year, temple donations, mining and quarrying expeditions, a naval raid on two Levantine towns bringing back over 1,500 captives, and tribute from Asiatic rulers. It is the fullest surviving royal account of what a Middle Kingdom state actually did with its revenue.
entries.note: Mit Rahina (Memphis) annal fragments: Malek & Quirke, 'Memphis 1991: epigraphy', JEA 78 (1992); Altenmüller & Moussa, 'Die Inschrift Amenemhets II. aus dem Ptah-Tempel von Memphis', SAK 18 (1991). The Tôd treasure was deposited under his name (see Exchange). Grajetzki (2006) pp.42–44.

entries.label: Senwosret II — the turn to the Faiyum
entries.hint: Khakheperre Senwosret II moved the royal burial ground south to el-Lahun at the mouth of the Faiyum depression and began the hydraulic works — regulating the Bahr Yusuf channel and the inflow to Lake Moeris — that his successors turned into Egypt's largest land-reclamation project. Beside his pyramid his officials laid out the planned town now called Kahun, whose discarded papyri are a primary source for Middle Kingdom administration, medicine and mathematics.
entries.note: El-Lahun pyramid, town and papyri: W.M.F. Petrie, Kahun, Gurob and Hawara (1890) and Illahun, Kahun and Gurob (1891). Papyri published by Borchardt, Griffith (Hieratic Papyri from Kahun and Gurob, 1898) and, recently, Collier & Quirke (2002–06). Grajetzki (2006) pp.45–47.

entries.label: Senwosret III — breaking the nomarchs, holding Nubia
entries.hint: Khakaure Senwosret III campaigned into Nubia at least four times and fixed the border at Semna with a pair of boundary stelae forbidding any Nehesy to pass north except to trade or on embassy. In the same reign the great provincial-governor tombs of Middle Egypt — at Beni Hasan, el-Bersha, Qau — abruptly stop being built, the sign historians read as a deliberate curbing of hereditary nomarch power in favour of central departments. He was worshipped as a god in Nubia for centuries afterward and his drawn, heavy-lidded portrait sculpture broke with the serene royal ideal.
entries.note: Semna boundary stelae (Berlin 1157, year 16; Berlin 14753). Nubian fort dispatches (the 'Semna Despatches', P. BM 10752). Decline of nomarch tombs: Grajetzki (2006) pp.48–55; Franke, 'The Career of Khnumhotep III', in Quirke (ed.), Middle Kingdom Studies (1991). Mortuary complex at Abydos: Josef Wegner, The Mortuary Temple of Senwosret III at Abydos (2007).

entries.label: Amenemhat III — the Faiyum at its height
entries.hint: Nimaatre Amenemhat III reigned some forty-five years, most of them in peace, and completed the Faiyum project: new dykes and sluices, reclaimed farmland, the twin colossi of Biahmu, and a temple to the crocodile god Sobek and the harvest goddess Renenutet at Medinet Maadi. His pyramid at Hawara was fronted by a vast columned mortuary complex that Herodotus and Strabo, seeing its ruins, called 'the Labyrinth' and rated above the pyramids themselves. He also drove Sinai turquoise and Hammamat greywacke mining to its Middle Kingdom peak.
entries.note: Hawara pyramid and 'Labyrinth': Petrie, Hawara, Biahmu and Arsinoe (1889); Herodotus 2.148, Strabo 17.1.37. Medinet Maadi (Narmouthis) temple: Achille Vogliano's excavations, 1935–39. Sinai: Serabit el-Khadim inscriptions, Gardiner, Peet & Černý, The Inscriptions of Sinai (1952–55). Grajetzki (2006) pp.56–58.

entries.label: Amenemhat IV and Sobekneferu — the dynasty's quiet close
entries.hint: Maakherure Amenemhat IV reigned about nine years, sending the usual Sinai and Punt-route expeditions and finishing the Medinet Maadi temple. He left no surviving son, and the throne passed to Sobekneferu — the first woman to rule Egypt as a titled king whose reign is beyond doubt, given roughly four years by the Turin Canon. With her death the Twelfth Dynasty ended and the fast turnover of the Thirteenth began, though without any recorded rupture.
entries.note: Turin Canon column 6 gives Sobekneferu 3 years 10 months 24 days. Sobekneferu's statuary: fragments in the Louvre (E 27135) and Berlin combining male kingly dress with female form. Amenemhat IV's Sinai stelae: Inscriptions of Sinai nos.118–122. Grajetzki (2006) pp.58–61; Ryholt, The Political Situation in Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period (1997) pp.209–13.

entries.label: The Thirteenth Dynasty — many kings, one bureaucracy
entries.hint: The Turin Canon lists roughly fifty kings for the Thirteenth Dynasty across about 125 years — most reigning only a year or two, few related to their predecessors — while the same viziers, treasurers and the powerful family of the vizier Ankhu kept the state running from Itjtawy. The ablest kings, Neferhotep I and his brother Sobekhotep IV, still commanded respect at Byblos and built at Karnak and Abydos, but through the period the eastern Delta slipped out of central control.
entries.note: Turin Canon columns 6–8. Neferhotep I: the Abydos stela (Cairo JE 6307) forbidding building in the sacred zone; a rock relief at Byblos showing the local ruler Yantinu enthroned below Neferhotep's cartouche. Reconstruction: Ryholt, The Political Situation in Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period (1997) pp.9–29, 213–48; Grajetzki (2006) pp.62–69.

entries.label: The Fourteenth Dynasty — a Canaanite line at Avaris
entries.hint: While the Thirteenth Dynasty still ruled from Itjtawy, a separate line of kings with West Semitic names — the best attested is Nehesy — governed the eastern Delta from Avaris, where excavation has traced a large immigrant Canaanite population with its own temple architecture, weapons and burial customs. Known almost entirely from scarab seals and the Turin Canon, this Fourteenth Dynasty shows the Delta already politically detached from the Nile Valley a generation before the Hyksos.
entries.note: Turin Canon columns 8–9 (a long list of largely Semitic names). Nehesy: monuments reused at Tell el-Dab'a, Tell el-Muqdam and Bubastis. Archaeology: Manfred Bietak, Avaris: The Capital of the Hyksos (1996) and the Tell el-Dab'a excavation reports. Reconstruction: Ryholt (1997) pp.94–116, 409–10.

entries.label: Salitis — the founding of the Hyksos kingdom
entries.hint: Manetho, quoted by Josephus, has a ruler named Salitis seize Memphis and make the eastern-Delta city of Avaris his fortified capital, founding the line the Egyptians called the heqau khasut, 'rulers of foreign lands' — Hyksos. The takeover ended native rule over Lower Egypt for about a century. Whether it was a single conquest or the seizure of power by an already-settled Canaanite elite is debated, but Memphis clearly fell and the Thirteenth Dynasty retreated south.
entries.note: Manetho via Josephus, Contra Apionem 1.75–92 (the term Hyksos and the Avaris account). The early Hyksos king Sakir-Har is attested on a doorjamb from Tell el-Dab'a. Discussion: Bourriau, 'The Second Intermediate Period', in Shaw (ed.), Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000) pp.185–95; Ryholt (1997) pp.118–50.

entries.label: Khyan — a Hyksos king known from Crete to the Tigris
entries.hint: Seuserenre Khyan is the Hyksos king whose seal impressions and small objects turn up most widely outside Egypt — at Knossos on Crete, at Hattusa in Anatolia, and (a lid with his name) at Baghdad — evidence of the trade reach of an Avaris-based state. Sealings found at Tell Edfu in a Thirteenth-Dynasty administrative context have pushed his date earlier than once thought, so that he may have overlapped a still-functioning native dynasty rather than following it.
entries.note: Khyan objects: the Knossos lid (Evans, The Palace of Minos I, 1921); the Hattusa fragment; the Baghdad lid. Tell Edfu sealings: Nadine Moeller & Gregory Marouard, 'Discussion of Late Middle Kingdom and Early Second Intermediate Period History...', Ägypten und Levante 21 (2011). Ryholt (1997) pp.256–58.

entries.label: Apepi — the last great Hyksos king
entries.hint: Aauserre Apepi reigned around forty years, long enough to use three different prenomens, and presided over the Hyksos kingdom at its height and into its war with Thebes. His name stands on the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus (copied in his Year 33), on monuments reused from earlier kings, and in the later folk tale 'The Quarrel of Apepi and Seqenenre', which blames the war's outbreak on his complaint about the noise of Theban hippopotami. A letter of his to the king of Kush, intercepted by Kamose, shows him seeking a two-front alliance against Thebes.
entries.note: Rhind Mathematical Papyrus (BM EA10057–10058), scribal note dating the copy to 'Year 33' of Apepi. 'Quarrel of Apepi and Seqenenre' (P. Sallier I, Ramesside). Intercepted letter: Second Kamose Stela. Apepi's daughter's writing-box and reused monuments. Ryholt (1997) pp.256–63; Bourriau in Shaw (2000) pp.196–99.

entries.label: The Sixteenth Dynasty — a Theban kingdom under pressure
entries.hint: After the Hyksos took Memphis, a line of minor Theban kings — Nebiriau I, Neferhotep III and others named mainly on stelae and the Turin Canon — held Upper Egypt from Thebes as a rump state. Neferhotep III's stela speaks of a city 'engulfed' and provisioned under threat, and famine and Hyksos raids in this window are visible archaeologically. Kim Ryholt separates these kings as a distinct Sixteenth Dynasty; others fold them into the Seventeenth.
entries.note: Turin Canon column 11. Stela of Neferhotep III (Cairo JE 59635). The Kamose texts look back on a time when Egypt was split three ways — Thebes, Avaris and Kush. Ryholt (1997) pp.151–66, 202; contra, Bourriau in Shaw (2000) pp.191–94.

entries.label: The early Seventeenth Dynasty — Rahotep to Sobekemsaf
entries.hint: The Seventeenth Dynasty rebuilt Theban kingship: Rahotep restored temples at Abydos and Koptos, Nubkheperre Intef issued a decree from Koptos removing a corrupt official and left a well-documented tomb at Dra Abu el-Naga, and Sobekemsaf II's rock-cut tomb was rich enough that its robbery, centuries later, became the subject of a Ramesside investigation papyrus. These kings still buried at Thebes in modest rishi coffins but were rearming for the war their successors would fight.
entries.note: Coptos Decree of Nubkheperre Intef (Cairo JE 30770). Tomb robbery of Sobekemsaf II: Abbott Papyrus (BM EA10221) and Leopold II–Amherst Papyrus, recording the Ramesside trial. Dra Abu el-Naga royal tombs: German Archaeological Institute excavations under Daniel Polz. Ryholt (1997) pp.170–204.

entries.label: Seqenenre Tao — the king killed in the war
entries.hint: Seqenenre Tao opened, or at least escalated, the Theban war against Apepi. His mummy, found in the Deir el-Bahari royal cache, has catastrophic head wounds — from an axe, a spear and a dagger of Levantine type, several delivered while he was already down — and no sign of embalming care at the point of death, consistent with a king killed on campaign and buried in haste. His queen Ahhotep and sons Kamose and Ahmose carried on the fight.
entries.note: Mummy (Cairo CG 61051), from the Deir el-Bahari cache (TT320). Forensic re-examination: G. Elliot Smith, The Royal Mummies (1912); recent CT study, Sahar Saleem & Zahi Hawass, Scanning the Pharaohs (2016) pp.61–70. Ryholt (1997) pp.170–72.

entries.label: Kamose — the campaign to Avaris
entries.hint: Wadjkheperre Kamose, Seqenenre's son or brother, reigned only about three years but left two large stelae at Karnak narrating a campaign that swept the Hyksos vassal Teti son of Pepi out of Nefrusy, raided the fields around Avaris itself, and intercepted a courier carrying Apepi's plea for help to the king of Kush. Kamose died before the city fell; his brother Ahmose completed the expulsion around 1550, opening the New Kingdom.
entries.note: First and Second Kamose Stelae (Karnak; the second, Cairo Temp. No. 11/1/35/1, found reused in a Ramesside statue base), with the Carnavon Tablet I school copy. Translation: Simpson (ed.), The Literature of Ancient Egypt (2003) pp.345–50. Ryholt (1997) pp.172–74; Grajetzki (2006) pp.70–71.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The wars of reunification, the conquest of Lower Nubia, and the Theban war against the Hyksos

entries.label: Mentuhotep II defeats Herakleopolis
entries.hint: The decisive phase of the civil war between the Theban Eleventh Dynasty and the Herakleopolitan kings ended with Mentuhotep II in control of the whole country. A mass tomb at Deir el-Bahari held about sixty men killed by arrows and blunt force, some with arrows still in the body, wrapped and carried home for honourable burial near the king's temple — most likely soldiers who fell storming Herakleopolis or a northern fortress.
entries.note: Tomb of the sixty soldiers (MMA 507), Deir el-Bahari: excavated by Herbert Winlock, 1926–27; Winlock, The Slain Soldiers of Neb-hepet-Re Mentu-hotpe (1945). Reunification date from regnal-year titulary changes; Grajetzki (2006) pp.19–24.

entries.label: Senwosret I annexes Lower Nubia to the Second Cataract
entries.hint: In his 18th year Senwosret I's army, under the general Mentuhotep, 'sailed south to overthrow Wawat', and Egypt annexed Lower Nubia outright, replacing raids with occupation. A ring of mudbrick fortresses — Buhen, Ikkur, Kuban, Aniba — was built or rebuilt to garrison the river, protect the desert gold mines and channel Nubian trade through Egyptian checkpoints.
entries.note: Buhen stela of Mentuhotep and the Girgawi rock inscription (year 18). Fortress sequence: W.B. Emery, H.S. Smith & A. Millard, The Fortress of Buhen (1979); Lawrence, 'Ancient Egyptian Fortifications', JEA 51 (1965). Grajetzki (2006) pp.37–40.

entries.label: Senwosret III's Nubian wars and the Semna line
entries.hint: Senwosret III led armies into Nubia in his 8th, 10th, 16th and 19th years, dredged a bypass canal at the First Cataract to move warships upstream, and drew the frontier at Semna. His Year 16 boundary stela sets out an explicitly aggressive doctrine — hold the line, raid the enemy's wells and crops, take his women — and calls the Nubian a coward who 'retreats when one is fierce against him'. The new forts at Semna, Kumma, Uronarti and Shalfak sealed the cataract.
entries.note: Semna boundary stelae, Year 16 (Berlin ÄM 1157) and Year 8 (Berlin ÄM 14753); translation in Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature I (1973) pp.118–20. First Cataract canal: Sehel inscription. Fortress archaeology: G.A. Reisner's Semna–Kumma excavations, published Dunham & Janssen (1960).

entries.label: Khusobek and the campaign against Sekmem
entries.hint: The autobiographical stela of Khusobek (also read Sebek-khu), a soldier who rose through the ranks under Senwosret III, records the king leading an army into Retjenu and a fight at a place called Sekmem, usually identified with Shechem — the earliest specific, named Egyptian military engagement in the Levant rather than a generic 'smiting of Asiatics'. Khusobek fought in the rearguard, was decorated, and set his stela up at Abydos.
entries.note: Stela of Khusobek (Manchester Museum 3306), from Abydos; T. Eric Peet, The Stela of Sebek-khu (1914); translation in Simpson (ed.), The Literature of Ancient Egypt (2003) pp.421–22. Context: Grajetzki (2006) pp.53–54.

entries.label: The Hyksos take Memphis and the Delta
entries.hint: Over the late Thirteenth Dynasty the eastern Delta passed first to the Canaanite Fourteenth Dynasty and then to the Hyksos, who took Memphis and pushed the native kings back to the Thebaid. Manetho remembered a violent sack; the archaeology at Avaris shows instead a large settled immigrant population whose leaders assumed pharaonic titles. Either way, by about 1650 BC Egypt was partitioned — Hyksos in the north, Thebes in the south, and the kingdom of Kush beyond the Second Cataract.
entries.note: Manetho via Josephus, Contra Apionem 1.75–92. Demographic evidence: Bietak, Avaris: The Capital of the Hyksos (1996). Partition described retrospectively in the Kamose stelae. Bourriau in Shaw (ed.), Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000) pp.185–99.

entries.label: The Theban war against the Hyksos
entries.hint: The Seventeenth Dynasty's war to reunite Egypt runs from Seqenenre Tao — killed in the fighting — through Kamose's northern raid to the fields of Avaris and the interception of Apepi's letter to Kush, and ends with Ahmose's capture of Avaris and pursuit of the Hyksos into southern Canaan around 1550 BC. The soldier Ahmose son of Ibana, of el-Kab, recorded the siege of Avaris and the storming of Sharuhen in his tomb autobiography, the fullest eyewitness account of the campaign's close.
entries.note: Kamose stelae (Karnak); autobiography of Ahmose son of Ibana, tomb at el-Kab (translation, Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II, 1976, pp.12–15) — the fall of Avaris and Sharuhen belong to Ahmose I's reign, just past this folio's close. Seqenenre's wounds: Saleem & Hawass, Scanning the Pharaohs (2016).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The move to Itjtawy, the mature vizierate, Senwosret III's provincial reform and the fortress administration of Nubia

entries.label: Itjtawy and the rebuilt central state
entries.hint: Amenemhat I pulled the administration out of Thebes into a purpose-built residence, Itjtawy, sited between Memphis and the Faiyum so a single court could reach both halves of the country. The First Intermediate Period's independent regional treasuries gave way again to a central treasury, a granary administration and a labour bureau, and a royal progress recorded in the Prophecy of Neferti frames the new order as the restoration of maat after chaos.
entries.note: Itjtawy is not yet located; its cemeteries at el-Lisht (pyramids of Amenemhat I and Senwosret I) fix it approximately. Prophecy of Neferti (P. Leningrad 1116B): Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature I (1973) pp.139–45. Administrative synthesis: Quirke, The Administration of Egypt in the Late Middle Kingdom (1990) pp.1–20.

entries.label: The vizierate and Papyrus Boulaq 18
entries.hint: By the late Middle Kingdom the vizier (tjaty) ran the civil state day to day, and one office-holder, Ankhu, was powerful enough that his family supplied viziers across several short-lived Thirteenth-Dynasty reigns. Papyrus Boulaq 18, a set of accounts from the Theban royal palace, lists the court in session under the vizier — rations issued, officials present, a visiting delegation of Nubians — the most detailed surviving snapshot of a Middle Kingdom government at work.
entries.note: Papyrus Boulaq 18 (Cairo CG 58069): Scharff, 'Ein Rechnungsbuch des königlichen Hofes', ZÄS 57 (1922); re-edition Quirke, In the House of Osiris (2004). Vizier Ankhu: Ryholt, The Political Situation in Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period (1997) pp.216–17; Quirke, Administration of Egypt in the Late Middle Kingdom (1990).

entries.label: Senwosret III's departmental reform
entries.hint: Under Senwosret III the country was run through three great departments (waret) — of the North, of the South, and of the 'Head of the South' covering Elephantine and Lower Nubia — each under a reporting official answering to the vizier. In the same reign the monumental tombs of the hereditary provincial governors of Middle Egypt cease abruptly, the change usually read as the crown replacing inherited nomarch power with appointed, salaried departmental officers.
entries.note: The waret structure is reconstructed from title strings on late Middle Kingdom seals and stelae: Quirke, The Administration of Egypt in the Late Middle Kingdom (1990) pp.35–75. End of the great nomarch tombs at Beni Hasan, Deir el-Bersha, Qau, Meir: Grajetzki, The Middle Kingdom of Ancient Egypt (2006) pp.49–52; Willems, Dayr al-Barsha I (2007).

entries.label: The Semna Despatches
entries.hint: A papyrus roll copied at Thebes preserves a run of routine reports sent downstream from the Second Cataract forts: patrols tracking the tracks of desert nomads, a party of Medjay who 'came to serve' and were turned back, boats logged past the checkpoint, a note that 'all the affairs of the King's domain are safe and sound'. It is the earliest surviving military field correspondence from anywhere, and shows the fortresses working as a permeable trade-and-surveillance line, not a wall.
entries.note: The Semna Despatches (P. BM EA10752, verso; the Ramesseum papyri find): P.C. Smither, 'The Semnah Despatches', JEA 31 (1945). Context: Kemp, 'Old Kingdom, Middle Kingdom and Second Intermediate Period', in Trigger et al., Ancient Egypt: A Social History (1983) pp.130–36.

entries.label: Household registers and bonded labour
entries.hint: Middle Kingdom paperwork tracked people closely. Census scraps from Kahun list each household head with dependants, lodgers and servants; the Thirteenth-Dynasty Brooklyn Papyrus carries a roster of about ninety-five labourers assigned to one estate, roughly half of them bearing Asiatic names and glossed with Egyptian ones, alongside royal decrees on the pursuit of people who fled compulsory labour. Together they document a legal category of hereditary service short of chattel slavery.
entries.note: Kahun census fragments: Griffith, Hieratic Papyri from Kahun and Gurob (1898); Collier & Quirke, The UCL Lahun Papyri (2002–06). Brooklyn Papyrus 35.1446: William C. Hayes, A Papyrus of the Late Middle Kingdom in the Brooklyn Museum (1955). Discussion: Loprieno & Schneider (eds.), various; Grajetzki (2006) pp.140–46.

entries.label: Co-regency as a device for the succession
entries.hint: Amenemhat I raised his son Senwosret I to joint kingship in what most Egyptologists read as the first co-regency, with documents double-dated to both reigns and the Story of Sinuhe turning on the moment the news of Amenemhat's murder reaches the co-regent on campaign. Amenemhat II, Senwosret II and Senwosret III appear to have repeated the arrangement, using it to pre-empt disputed transfers of power — a Twelfth-Dynasty institutional signature, though a minority of scholars dispute that true joint rule occurred.
entries.note: Double-dated stela of Semna (year 30 of Amenemhat I = year 10 of Senwosret I). Story of Sinuhe R5–17. The case for and against: W.J. Murnane, Ancient Egyptian Coregencies (1977); Claude Obsomer, Sésostris Ier (1995) argues against a formal Amenemhat I / Senwosret I coregency. Grajetzki (2006) pp.30–36.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Osiris at Abydos, the Coffin Texts and the democratised afterlife, and the rise of Amun of Thebes

entries.label: The mysteries of Osiris at Abydos
entries.hint: Abydos became the ritual centre of the Osiris cult. Each year a procession carried the god's image from his temple out to the desert tomb identified as his burial and back, re-enacting his death, vindication and revival; private people crowded the processional route with small offering chapels so their own memorial stones would 'see' the god pass. The official Ikhernofret's stela records Senwosret III sending him to re-equip the cult image in gold and electrum and to play a leading role in the festival.
entries.note: Ikhernofret stela (Berlin ÄM 1204), from Abydos; translation Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature I (1973) pp.123–25. The votive chapel zone ('Terrace of the Great God'): Simpson, The Terrace of the Great God at Abydos (1974); O'Connor, Abydos (2009) pp.89–110.

entries.label: The Coffin Texts and the Book of Two Ways
entries.hint: Spells once reserved for the king's pyramid were now painted inside the wooden coffins of provincial officials and their families — over a thousand distinct 'Coffin Texts' — extending a guided afterlife to anyone who could afford a decorated coffin. On the floor-boards of coffins from Deir el-Bersha appears the Book of Two Ways, the earliest known illustrated map of the netherworld, charting water and fire routes past demons to the realm of Osiris.
entries.note: Adriaan de Buck, The Egyptian Coffin Texts, 7 vols. (1935–61). Book of Two Ways: Leonard Lesko, The Ancient Egyptian Book of Two Ways (1972); the Bersha coffins were excavated by Daressy and later the Harvard–Boston expedition (1915). Willems, Chests of Life (1988).

entries.label: Amun of Thebes rises to national god
entries.hint: A once-minor Theban deity, Amun ('the hidden one'), was promoted by the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties into a supreme creator, fused with the sun as Amun-Ra. Senwosret I built the first substantial stone temple to him at Karnak, with a limestone kiosk (the 'White Chapel') for the god's bark, and the throne name borne by four Twelfth-Dynasty kings, Amenemhat, means 'Amun is at the fore'. The Theban god's national standing set here would underwrite the New Kingdom empire.
entries.note: White Chapel of Senwosret I: reconstructed from ~350 blocks recovered from the Third Pylon fill at Karnak; P. Lacau & H. Chevrier, Une chapelle de Sésostris Ier à Karnak (1956–69). Middle Kingdom court at Karnak: Centre Franco-Égyptien d'Étude des Temples de Karnak excavations, Luc Gabolde, Le 'grand château d'Amon' de Sésostris Ier à Karnak (1998).

entries.label: The votive stela and appeals to the god
entries.hint: Middle Kingdom Egyptians of modest means increasingly set up their own inscribed stelae — most densely at Abydos — asking a named god directly for a good burial, offerings, and remembrance, and sometimes admitting fault and asking mercy. This more personal, less strictly royal-mediated relationship with the divine, together with household protective figures of Bes, Taweret and the cobra-goddess Renenutet, is visible well before the 'personal piety' usually associated with the later New Kingdom.
entries.note: Abydos votive stelae corpus: numbering in the thousands, dispersed to museums from 19th-century digging; Simpson, The Terrace of the Great God at Abydos (1974). Household cult objects: Geraldine Pinch, Votive Offerings to Hathor (1993); Stephen Quirke, Exploring Religion in Ancient Egypt (2015) pp.90–120.

entries.label: The pyramid returns — Lisht, Lahun, Hawara, Dahshur
entries.hint: The Twelfth Dynasty revived royal pyramid burial after the First Intermediate gap, but built cheaply: rubble or mudbrick cores behind a stone casing, with elaborate hidden passages, blocking portcullises and dead-end shafts meant to defeat robbers. Senwosret III at Dahshur, Amenemhat III first at Dahshur and then at Hawara, each endowed a cult town of priests and workers to keep the offerings going. Amenemhat III's Hawara mortuary temple, seen in ruins by Greek visitors, was remembered as 'the Labyrinth'.
entries.note: Pyramid archaeology: Dieter Arnold, The Pyramid Complex of Senwosret III at Dahshur (2002); Petrie, Kahun, Gurob and Hawara (1890) and Hawara, Biahmu and Arsinoe (1889). Overview: Mark Lehner, The Complete Pyramids (1997) pp.168–83.

entries.label: Sobek and the temple of Medinet Maadi
entries.hint: As the crown poured resources into the Faiyum, the local crocodile god Sobek — lord of the marshes and the waters — rose with it, often merged with the sun as Sobek-Ra. Amenemhat III and Amenemhat IV built him and the harvest-goddess Renenutet a small stone temple at Medinet Maadi on the southwest edge of the cultivation; buried by sand and reoccupied in Ptolemaic times, it is the most completely preserved temple to survive from the Middle Kingdom.
entries.note: Medinet Maadi (ancient Dja, Greek Narmouthis): excavated by Achille Vogliano for the University of Milan, 1935–39; ongoing work by the Università di Pisa. Marco Zecchi, Geografia religiosa del Fayyum (2001) and A Study of the Egyptian God Osiris; Bresciani & Giammarusti, I templi di Medinet Madi (2012).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Classical Middle Egyptian and the golden age of Egyptian literature; the careworn royal portrait

entries.label: Classical Middle Egyptian
entries.hint: The written language of the Middle Kingdom became the standard that later Egyptians measured themselves against: temple inscriptions were still being composed in imitation of it under the Ptolemies and Romans, more than 1,500 years on. Its literature was copied and re-copied as school texts through the New Kingdom, which is why so much of it survives. Alongside it a cursive 'hieratic' book-hand matured for writing on papyrus at speed.
entries.note: Standard grammar: Alan Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar (3rd ed. 1957); James P. Allen, Middle Egyptian (2000). On its status as the classical register: Antonio Loprieno, Ancient Egyptian: A Linguistic Introduction (1995) pp.5–8.

entries.label: The Story of Sinuhe
entries.hint: An official flees Egypt in panic on hearing of Amenemhat I's assassination, makes a life among the pastoralists of Retjenu, defeats a local champion in single combat, and in old age is summoned home by Senwosret I to be buried as an Egyptian. Its psychological depth, its verse speeches, and its picture of the Levantine world make it the acknowledged masterwork of Egyptian literature; over thirty ancient copies are known.
entries.note: Principal manuscripts P. Berlin 3022 (Middle Kingdom) and P. Ashmolean 1945.40 (Ramesside). Editions: Roland Koch, Die Erzählung des Sinuhe (1990); translation and study, R.B. Parkinson, The Tale of Sinuhe and Other Ancient Egyptian Poems (1997) pp.21–53.

entries.label: The Tale of the Eloquent Peasant
entries.hint: A tradesman of the salt oasis is robbed on the road by a petty official's servant and lays his case before the high steward Rensi in nine formal petitions of mounting rhetorical brilliance on justice, balance and the duty of the powerful. The official deliberately withholds judgement to keep the man talking, and the king has the speeches written down. It is Egyptian literature's fullest meditation on maat as a social obligation.
entries.note: Four Middle Kingdom manuscripts (P. Berlin 3023, 3025, 10499; P. Butler / BM 10274). Edition: R.B. Parkinson, The Tale of the Eloquent Peasant (1991); translation in Parkinson, The Tale of Sinuhe... (1997) pp.54–88.

entries.label: The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor
entries.hint: A sailor, sole survivor of a wreck, washes up on a vanishing island ruled by a giant golden serpent who foretells his rescue and sends him home laden with incense and marvels — a story told, as a frame, to console an official dreading a report to the king. It is the earliest fully preserved fantastic tale in world literature and survives in a single manuscript.
entries.note: Sole manuscript P. Hermitage (St Petersburg) 1115, discovered by Vladimir Golenishchev, published 1906. Translation: Parkinson, The Tale of Sinuhe and Other Ancient Egyptian Poems (1997) pp.89–101; Simpson (ed.), The Literature of Ancient Egypt (2003) pp.45–53.

entries.label: The literature of doubt and distress
entries.hint: A strand of Middle Kingdom writing turns inward and pessimistic: the Dialogue of a Man with his Ba weighs suicide against the fear of oblivion; the Admonitions of Ipuwer and the Prophecy of Neferti paint social order inverted, the poor made rich and the land in chaos; the Lament of Khakheperreseneb complains that everything worth saying has been said. Whether these describe the real First Intermediate collapse or use it as a literary setting is debated, but they gave Egypt a vocabulary for disorder.
entries.note: Dialogue of a Man with his Ba (P. Berlin 3024); Admonitions of Ipuwer (P. Leiden I 344 recto, a later copy); Prophecy of Neferti (P. Leningrad 1116B). Translations: Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature I (1973) pp.139–92; Parkinson, Voices from Ancient Egypt (1991).

entries.label: The careworn royal face
entries.hint: Sculptors working for Senwosret III and Amenemhat III produced royal heads unlike anything before: hooded, pouched eyes, deep lines from nose to mouth, an almost grim expression, sometimes on a body still shown as youthful and strong. The break from the ageless, serene ideal is deliberate and much argued over — an image of the sleepless burden of rule, of a king as careful shepherd, or of a new realism — but it is the Middle Kingdom's most distinctive contribution to Egyptian art.
entries.note: Key pieces: obsidian and quartzite heads of Senwosret III (Metropolitan Museum 26.7.1394; British Museum EA 686, from Abydos); sphinxes and statues of Amenemhat III from Tanis and the Faiyum (reused). Discussion: Fay, The Louvre Sphinx and Royal Sculpture from the Reign of Amenemhat II (1996); Dorothea Arnold, 'Royal Portraits of the Twelfth Dynasty', MMJ 26 (1991).

entries.label: The Lahun hymns and court performance
entries.hint: A papyrus from Kahun preserves a cycle of hymns hailing Senwosret III on his arrival at a town — 'Twice great is the king of his city!' — with repeated refrains built for choral delivery, the closest thing to a surviving Middle Kingdom song lyric. Tomb-chapel painting of the period, above all at Beni Hasan, shows the ensembles that performed such pieces: harpists, flute and double-pipe players, singers marking rhythm with hand-clappers.
entries.note: Hymns to Senwosret III: P. UC 32157 (Kahun); Griffith, Hieratic Papyri from Kahun and Gurob (1898) pp.1–3, pl.1–3; translation Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature I (1973) pp.198–201. Musicians: Newberry, Beni Hasan I–II (1893–94), tombs of Khnumhotep II and Amenemhat (BH2, BH3).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The mathematical and medical papyri, word-lists and the measurement of the sky

entries.label: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus
entries.date: c.1550 BC (copy of a c.1850 BC original)
entries.hint: The scribe Ahmose copied this 5-metre roll under the Hyksos king Apepi from a Twelfth-Dynasty original, opening it as 'the correct method of reckoning, for grasping the meaning of things'. Its 84 worked problems cover division into unit fractions (with a reference table for 2 ÷ odd numbers), the sharing of loaves and wages, the slope of pyramids, and the area of a circle by a rule equivalent to taking pi as about 3.16. It is the fullest source for how Egyptians actually did arithmetic.
entries.note: P. BM EA 10057 and 10058, said to be from a building near the Ramesseum; acquired by A.H. Rhind, 1858. Standard edition: T.E. Peet, The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus (1923); Robins & Shute, The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus: An Ancient Egyptian Text (1987).

entries.label: The Moscow Mathematical Papyrus and the frustum
entries.hint: This shorter roll's 25 problems include Problem 14, which computes the volume of a truncated square pyramid by a rule mathematically identical to the modern formula — evidence that Egyptian scribes could handle a genuinely three-dimensional result — and Problem 10, usually read as the area of a curved (basket or hemisphere) surface. It shows the practical geometry of a state that moved earth and stone by the cubic cubit.
entries.note: P. Moscow (Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts) 4676; acquired by Vladimir Golenishchev, 1892–93. Edition: W.W. Struve, Mathematischer Papyrus des Staatlichen Museums der Schönen Künste in Moskau (1930); Clagett, Ancient Egyptian Science III (1999).

entries.label: The Kahun Gynaecological Papyrus
entries.hint: The oldest surviving medical document from Egypt, found in the rubbish of the Lahun pyramid town: 34 short paragraphs on women's health — complaints traced to the womb, tests for fertility and for whether a woman will bear, and prescriptions including one of the earliest written references to a contraceptive. A companion Lahun papyrus does the same for the diseases of cattle, the earliest veterinary text.
entries.note: P. UC 32057 (Kahun Gynaecological Papyrus); Griffith, Hieratic Papyri from Kahun and Gurob (1898) pp.5–11. Veterinary papyrus: P. UC 32036. Re-edition: Collier & Quirke, The UCL Lahun Papyri: Religious, Literary, Legal, Mathematical and Medical (2004).

entries.label: The surgical tradition of the Edwin Smith Papyrus
entries.date: copy c.1600 BC; core often dated earlier
entries.hint: The Edwin Smith Papyrus, though physically a Second Intermediate Period copy, preserves a treatise whose composition many scholars place in the Middle Kingdom or before: 48 trauma cases ordered head-to-heel, each with examination, diagnosis, a verdict ('an ailment I will treat' / 'will contend with' / 'not to be treated'), and treatment. It contains the first written appearance of the word 'brain' and observations of paralysis linked to spinal injury, worked in an unusually detached, empirical style.
entries.note: P. Edwin Smith (New York Academy of Medicine), bought at Luxor 1862. Edition: James Henry Breasted, The Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus (1930). On the disputed composition date: Allen, The Art of Medicine in Ancient Egypt (2005) pp.70–71.

entries.label: Star-clocks and the hours of the night
entries.hint: Coffin lids of Middle Kingdom officials, best known from Asyut, carry grids that list 36 star-groups (decans) against the ten-day 'weeks' of the year, so that the rising of a given decan told the hour of the night — the earliest surviving apparatus for dividing darkness into hours, and the root of the 24-hour day. The same period standardised the 365-day civil calendar of three seasons for administrative use, alongside word-lists that catalogued the ordered world by category.
entries.note: Diagonal star tables: Otto Neugebauer & Richard Parker, Egyptian Astronomical Texts I: The Early Decans (1960). Word-lists: the Ramesseum Onomasticon (a Middle Kingdom papyrus from the Ramesseum tomb group), Gardiner, Ancient Egyptian Onomastica (1947).
